knowledgeComponents.description: Add or subtract fractions that already share a common denominator by operating only on the numerators.

basis: 0 of 0 evidence spans matched the snapshot

prerequisiteEdges.justification: Finding a common multiple so fractions can be compared or equated first requires knowing that only numerators change once denominators already match.
Simplifying is the reverse of generating equivalents: the learner must already see that multiplying or dividing both terms by the same number leaves the value unchanged.
Writing 16/100 as 4/25 (or 0.16 as 16%) depends on reducing or expanding the same rational number.
A ratio such as 1:2 is interpreted as 1/3 and 2/3 of the whole only after the learner can treat those fractions as equivalent parts of a common whole.
Sharing $20 in the ratio 2:3 requires first knowing there are 5 equal parts before assigning values to those parts.
Practical modelling (mixes, concentrations, recipes) applies the same share-in-ratio calculation inside a real context and then interprets the result.
Contexts such as 1:4 concentrate as 0.2 of the mixture require converting the part–whole fraction into a decimal or percent to compute and communicate the answer.

misconceptions.label: Adds both numerators and denominators
misconceptions.description: When combining or generating fractions the learner writes a/b + c/d = (a+c)/(b+d) or treats 2/3 as becoming 2+4 / 3+4.

misconceptions.label: Reads ratio as a single fraction of one part
misconceptions.description: Interprets 1:4 as one-quarter of the whole rather than 1 part out of 5, so the complementary part is lost.

misconceptions.label: Splits by the ratio numbers without finding parts
misconceptions.description: Given $20 in the ratio 2:3, gives $2 and $3 (or $2 and $18) instead of finding the value of one of five equal parts.

options.rationale: Multiplying numerator and denominator by 2 gives 4/10.
Adds 2 to both the numerator and the denominator.
Adds 4 to both the numerator and the denominator.

items.keyRationale: Equivalent fractions are made by multiplying (or dividing) the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number.

options.rationale: Divide numerator and denominator by their highest common factor, 6.
Adds 2 to both the numerator and the denominator instead of dividing.
Adds 6 to both the numerator and the denominator instead of dividing.

items.keyRationale: Simplest form is found by dividing both parts of the fraction by the same common divisor until they share no common factor greater than 1.

options.rationale: Writes the digits of the fraction as a percentage without converting.
Places a decimal point between the digits instead of converting.
Multiplies 3 by 5 and writes the product as a percentage.

items.keyRationale: Divide 3 by 5 to get 0.6, then multiply by 100 to express the same value as 60%.

rejection.reason: Every incorrect option names a known misconception: 3 distractors have no known misconception: item:au.year-7.mathematics.fraction-decimal-percent-equivalence.01/B, item:au.year-7.mathematics.fraction-decimal-percent-equivalence.01/C, item:au.year-7.mathematics.fraction-decimal-percent-equivalence.01/D. Rejected rather than repaired.

items.stem: Paint is mixed in the ratio red : blue = 1 : 4. What fraction of the whole mixture is red?

options.rationale: There are 1 + 4 = 5 equal parts in total, so red is 1 of 5 parts.
Treats the ratio 1:4 as the fraction 1/4 of the whole and loses the complementary part.
Reads the second number as the whole instead of adding both parts.

items.keyRationale: A part–part ratio a:b has a + b parts in the whole, so the first colour is a/(a+b) of the mixture.

items.stem: Share $40 in the ratio 3 : 5. How much is the larger share?

options.rationale: 3 + 5 = 8 parts; one part is $5; five parts are $25.
Gives the ratio number 5 as dollars instead of finding the value of one of eight parts.
Gives the ratio number 3 as dollars instead of finding equal parts of $40.

items.keyRationale: Add the ratio parts, divide the total by that number, then multiply by 5 to get the larger share.

items.stem: A cordial recipe uses 2 parts concentrate to 7 parts water. How much concentrate is needed to make 450 mL of drink?

options.rationale: Uses 2 parts out of 7 instead of 2 parts out of 9.
Finds one part but does not scale by 2.
Gives the water amount instead of the concentrate.

items.keyRationale: Model the drink as 9 equal parts of 50 mL and take 2 of those parts for the concentrate.
